Reviews

Experimental

Marty Supreme (Original Soundtrack)

Daniel Lopatin
Best New Album
The electronic composer meets the larger-than-life film on its level, building the palette he’s honed over the years into a totalizing prism of sound.
Electronic

Implosion

The Bug / Ghost Dubs
The dub veterans bring out the best in each other with a collaborative album that balances lumbering doom with spacey ambience.
Rap

Soulja Hate Repellant

Niontay
One of MIKE’s roster of rap mavericks, Niontay probes the deepest, murkiest corners of his sound on this 454-hosted mixtape, blurring his influences and slurring his bars with abandon.
Folk/Country

Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares

Bulgarian State Radio & Television Female Vocal Choir
Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we look back on a collection of Communist-era Bulgarian folk recordings that became an unlikely hit for 4AD in the 1980s.
Jazz

You Want That Too!

Max Jaffe
With assists from Jeff Parker, Meg Duffy, and others, the versatile drummer’s latest album stakes its claim at the shifting border between jazz and electronic music.

More Reviews

  • Experimental

    Tranquilizer

    Oneohtrix Point Never
    Best New Album
    Drawing on a cache of commercial sample CDs, Daniel Lopatin assembles an impossibly dense and transportive electronic album that takes impermanence as its inspiration.
  • Pop/R&B

    Addison

    Addison Rae
    The girlypop album of summer warrants comparison to Lana, Madonna, and most of all, Britney. Are we ready for Addison?
  • Rock

    Snocaps

    Snocaps
    The Crutchfield twins—accompanied by MJ Lenderman and Brad Cook—reunite for a spirited new project that plays to their strengths and embraces all the miles they’ve traveled.
  • Pop/R&B

    LUX

    Rosalía
    Best New Album
    The Spanish singer’s fourth record is a heartfelt offering of avant-garde classical pop that roars through genre, romance, and religion.
  • Rap

    Stardust

    Danny Brown
    Working with a new vanguard of outsider electronic artists, the Detroit rapper lets his freak flag fry. The results are shaky but full of heart.
  • Pop/R&B

    West End Girl

    Lily Allen
    With an album that doubles as an insider’s account of a tabloid divorce, the singer finds a new evolution of her signature style: Lightness isn’t a foil for irony, but a vehicle for hurt.
  • Rap

    Lil Herb

    G Herbo
    Stepping into his teenage shoes for a loose concept album, the Chicago icon reflects on the original era of drill with the clarity of a scene veteran.
  • Electronic

    Repulsor

    Shlohmo
    The L.A. beatmaker turns aggressive on his fourth album—dialing up the distortion, flooding his beats with overdriven synths, and pushing anxious moods into the red.

Sunday Reviews

  • Rock

    Suburban Tours

    Rangers
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a DIY gem that funneled childhood nostalgia and omnivorous taste through piles of reverb and dirt-cheap equipment to become one of the great guitar records of the 21st century.
  • Rock

    Ruby Vroom

    Soul Coughing
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today we revisit the 1994 debut album from a New York group that mixed up rock, jazz, hip-hop beats, and slam poetry into a brand-new sound that is inextricably linked to its era.
  • Experimental
     / 
    Rock

    Strangers From the Universe

    Thinking Fellers Union Local 282
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit an essential talisman of freak music from 1994, a beautifully weird document of a beautifully weird band living out the last daydream of alternative rock.
  • Rock

    Giant Steps

    The Boo Radleys
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 1993 masterpiece from a group of shoegazing Beatles fanatics who went up against Oasis in the battle for the soul of British rock—and lost.
  • Rap

    Float

    Aesop Rock
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the 2000 record from the Long Island rapper, a deep, heady, and potent transmission from the splintering hip-hop underground.
  • Rock

    Horses

    Patti Smith
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit Patti Smith’s unparalleled debut, an album whose raw power and incalculable legacy catalyzed a new cultural order in music.
  • Rap

    Resurrection

    Common
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit the Chicago rapper’s second album, a powerful, multidimensional record that put the MC and his hometown on the map.
  • Metal

    Korn

    Korn
    Each Sunday, Pitchfork takes an in-depth look at a significant album from the past, and any record not in our archives is eligible. Today, we revisit a foundational nu metal album where a singer’s life of hurt and trauma gets weaponized by his band’s trailblazing sound.
